The science in brief Water clarity is one of our oldest and most intuitive lenses into aquatic ecosystems. For more than a century, hydrologists and limnologists have lowered Secchi disks into rivers, lakes, and estuaries to measure how deeply light penetrates the water column. Yet Secchi disk depth (\(z_{SD}\), in meters) alone tells us only how much light is lost—not what is blocking it. Across inland and coastal waters, diffuse light attenuation (\(k_d = 1 / z_{SD}\); Lee et al. 2015) is governed by pure water (\(k_w\)) and three primary light-attenuating constituents (LACs): non-algal particles (NAP), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and phytoplankton chlorophyll a (\(\text{Chl }a\)). Under the additive Beer–Lambert model, Secchi depth can be written directly in terms of constituent concentrations: \[z_{SD} = \frac{1}{k_w + \alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP} + \alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC} + \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a}\] To understand how these three constituents partition water clarity across the contiguous United States, we built an open-source pipeline on top of the AquaMatch data suite (Brousil et al. 2024a, 2024b, 2025; De La Torre et al. 2025)—the successor to AquaSat (Ross et al. 2019). Combining 276,321 simultaneous four-variable matchups (Secchi + Chl a + DOC + TSS/SSC) for model calibration with 484,723 three-constituent matchups across 39,595 monitoring stations (1970–2025), we estimate regional specific attenuation coefficients (\(\alpha_i\)) across U.S. EPA Level III ecoregions and project nearly half a million water quality observations into ternary attenuation space. Why Optical Partitioning & Total Visibility Both Matter ({sonicray} 3D Simulation) Ternary diagrams are a powerful way to visualize which constituent dominates light attenuation (\(f_{\text{NAP}} + f_{\text{DOC}} + f_{\text{Chl }a} = 1\)), but proportions alone miss a critical physical dimension: total visibility (\(z_{SD}\)). Two lakes sitting at the exact same coordinate in ternary space can represent either a crystal-clear oligotrophic basin (\(z_{SD} > 5\text{ m}\)) or a murky waterbody (\(z_{SD} < 0.4\text{ m}\)) when total constituent concentrations scale up. Moreover, each constituent alters the underwater light field in a distinct way: Chlorophyll a (Algae): Absorbs blue and red light while cells scatter green wavelengths, shifting water from deep blue to emerald green. DOC (Brownification): Absorbs short wavelengths exponentially with negligible particulate scattering, turning water into dark tea-stained blackwater. NAP / TSS (Sediment): Strongly backscatters broadband light, turning water chalky tan/ochre and driving the steepest collapse in Secchi visibility. Section 2 Simultaneous Matchups & Initial Hygiene (prep.R) To partition light attenuation among phytoplankton, non-algal particles, and dissolved organic carbon, we need field samples where chl_a, doc, and tss were collected on the same day at the same station (MonitoringLocationIdentifier and date)—which we refer to as matchups. Calibrating our bio-optical model additionally requires a same-day Secchi disk depth (secchi) measurement. am <- get_aquamatch() # 490,209 joined 3-LAC records (1970–2025) simul <- build_simultaneous(am, require_secchi = TRUE) no_secchi <- build_simultaneous(am, require_secchi = FALSE) 2.1 Four Initial Hygiene Filters Before statistical screening, build_simultaneous() in R/prep.R applies four simple, deterministic hygiene rules: Ambient water bodies only: Excludes industrial/municipal Facility outflows, retaining Estuary, Lake, and Stream sites. True Secchi measurements (for 4-variable calibration): Requires sdd_approx == 0 (excluding turbidity tubes) and sdd_mdl <= 1 (excluding \(\le 0.01\text{ m}\) floor placeholders). Section 3 Separating Non-Algal Particles (NAP) from Bulk TSS Our additive Beer–Lambert model partitions non-water light attenuation among three mutually exclusive pools: phytoplankton (Chl a), non-algal suspended particles (NAP: mineral sediment and detritus), and dissolved organic matter (DOC). Because standard gravimetric filtration measures bulk Total Suspended Solids (TSS)—which captures both mineral sediment and living algal cells on the filter—we subtract living phytoplankton dry mass from bulk TSS before fitting the model: Optical Component Field Measurement Model Predictor & Units Phytoplankton (\(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a\)) Chlorophyll a (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\text{mg m}^{-3} = \mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) used directly Non-algal particles (\(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP}\)) Bulk TSS / SSC (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - \text{biomass}(\text{Chl }a)\) (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) Dissolved organic matter (\(\alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC}\)) DOC (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{DOC}\) (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) used directly Following Gohin et al. (2005), we estimate phytoplankton dry biomass (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) from \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) as a power law that accounts for intracellular photoacclimation (lower carbon-to-chlorophyll ratios in nutrient-rich blooms; Geider et al. 1997; Cloern et al. 1995): \[\text{biomass}_{\text{algal}}\ [\text{mg L}^{-1}] = 0.234\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57}, \qquad \text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - 0.234\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57}\] Figure 3.1: (a) Empirical TSS vs. Chl a across matchups overlaid with the nonlinear Gohin et al. (2005) algal biomass curve (solid black) and constant linear dry-mass:Chl a ratios (dashed). We will never know the true dry-mass-to-chlorophyll ratio of the phytoplankton in each of these samples, so the useful question is how much the answer depends on it. Three things can be said. The ratio cannot be estimated from these data, and it does not affect the fit. For any constant ratio \(r\), \(\text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - r\,\text{Chl }a\), so \[k_d - k_w = \alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{TSS} + \alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC} + (\alpha_{\text{Chl }a} - r\,\alpha_{\text{NAP}})\,\text{Chl }a .\] That is the same regression on TSS, DOC and Chl a whatever \(r\) is. The fitted \(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\), \(\alpha_{\text{DOC}}\), \(R^2\) and every predicted Secchi depth are identical; only \(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\) shifts, by \(r\,\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\). The ratio decides how much of the particle attenuation is labelled algal, and nothing else. The data bound the ratio from above. Algal mass cannot exceed the suspended solids in the sample, so the low end of TSS : Chl a is an upper limit on the ratio. In lakes it falls as chlorophyll rises, which is the shape of the Gohin et al. (2005) relation; the Gohin curve sits at or below the 1st percentile, so it behaves as a lower bound on algal mass. A constant 100:1 is more than the total suspended solids present in roughly one in ten lake samples above \(100\ \mu\text{g L}^{-1}\). Section 4 Values Below Reporting Limits & Beer–Lambert Plausibility Screening Even after parameter and unit harmonization, roughly 2% of multi-agency WQP records contain field-recording or unit-entry anomalies that can heavily leverage ordinary least squares (OLS) slopes. However, simple marginal quantile trimming (clipping the top and bottom 0.1% or 1% of each variable independently) throws away genuine oligotrophic alpine lakes (Secchi up to 13.96 m) and real storm-flow sediment plumes (TSS up to 978 mg/L) while missing joint physical contradictions in the middle of the distribution. To clean recording errors without truncating real extremes or introducing statistical circularity, R/prep.R uses a two-stage protocol (n = 276,321): 4.1 Stage 1: Values Below Reporting Limits (trim_simultaneous()) Some Chl a, DOC and TSS values lie below the limits at which they can be reliably reported (Chl a 0.1 µg/L, DOC 0.25 mg/L, TSS 0.5 mg/L). They are kept, so all 281,439 simultaneous 4-variable matchups are retained, but they are not all given the value of the limit. Substituting the limit (or any other single number) for every such result distorts the low end of the distribution (Helsel 2006). Instead, following the “fill-in” approach of Lubin et al. (2004), each value below a limit is replaced by a random draw from a lognormal distribution that was fitted to that constituent by maximum likelihood for left-censored data and truncated at the limit (impute_lacs() in R/prep.R). Fewer than 3% of values are affected, well below the roughly 30% at which Lubin et al. found that the approach starts to bias variances. A screen that compares Secchi depth with a function of the three constituents, and then fits a model of the same form, invites two questions. Where do the reference numbers come from? And does the screen create the fit it is meant to protect? This section answers both. 4.3.1 Converting between attenuation and Secchi depth The published coefficients are per unit of diffuse attenuation \(K_d\). Our measurements are Secchi depths. The two are linked by (Eq. 1 of the manuscript) \[K_d = \frac{a}{z_{SD}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{z_{SD}} = \frac{K_d}{a}\] The factor \(a\) has a theoretical basis. A Secchi disk disappears at a depth set by the sum of the beam attenuation coefficient \(\alpha\) and the diffuse attenuation coefficient \(K\): \[z_{SD} = \frac{\Gamma}{\alpha + K}, \qquad \Gamma \approx 8 \text{ to } 9\] (Tyler 1968, Eq. 6, with \(\Gamma = 8.69\); Preisendorfer 1986, Eq. 55). Multiplying both sides by \(K\) gives \[a = K\,z_{SD} = \frac{\Gamma}{1 + \alpha/K}\] so \(a\) is small where scattering by particles makes \(\alpha\) large relative to \(K\), and large where absorption by colour dominates. Measured values agree: in 58 Alaskan lakes, \(K_d \times z_{SD}\) had a median of 1.86 in clear lakes, 0.93 in turbid lakes and 2.70 in stained lakes, and it ranged from 0.59 to 4.09 across 35 published studies (Koenings and Edmundson 1991, Table 2 and Table 6). Why the screen needs no conversion. If \(1/z_{SD} = K_d / a\), then for a matchup whose true attenuation equals the reference, \[r = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{1/z_{SD}}{K_{\text{ref}}}\right) = -\log_{10} a\] The screen uses \(z_r = (r - \bar r)/\text{SD}(r)\). A constant \(a\) changes every \(r\) by the same amount, changes \(\bar r\) by that amount too, and leaves \(z_r\) unchanged. Variation of \(a\) between waters remains in \(r\) and is part of what the 2.5 SD band has to accommodate. An independent check on the reference. The mean log ratio is \(\bar r = -0.255\), which corresponds to \(a = 10^{-\bar r} = 1.80\). Section 5 Hierarchical Ecoregion Stratification (ecoregions.R) A gram of dissolved organic carbon or suspended sediment does not attenuate the exact same amount of light everywhere. Humic DOC drained from northern peatlands is darker and more aromatic than autochthonous DOC in arid reservoirs (Spencer et al. 2012; Griffin et al. 2018), and fine clay suspensions scatter light much more efficiently per unit mass than coarse glacial silt (Bowers et al. 2020). To capture this regional biogeochemical coherence across streams, lakes, and estuaries within a single continental framework, eco_join() in R/ecoregions.R assigns each monitoring station (SiteID) to its nested U.S. EPA / CEC North American Ecoregion across Levels I–IV (Omernik & Griffith 2014). Nearshore estuarine stations located slightly seaward of coastline polygons are matched to the nearest coastal ecoregion via sf::st_nearest_feature(), guaranteeing a strict 1-to-1 mapping from SiteID to ecoregion. Section 7 Coefficient Stability & Sample-Size Convergence (Fig. S1) Do regional differences in fitted attenuation slopes (\(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}, \alpha_{\text{DOC}}, \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\)) reflect real biogeochemical differences across ecoregions, or just small-sample estimation noise? To answer this, we randomly partition the 276,321 training matchups into \(G\) subsets of varying sample size (\(n/50, n/100, \dots, n/10{,}000\), plus \(G=1\)) and refit the three-constituent model across 10 independent Monte Carlo replicates (random_subset_coefs() in R/models.R, seed P$random_seed = 20240826). Figure 7.1: Figure S1: Coefficient coherence cones across sample sizes. Grey ribbons span the 0.001%–99.999% quantiles of slopes fitted to random subsets of size n across all data and by water-body type. Colored circles mark Level III ecoregion fits (Models 7 and 8). Once group sample size exceeds \(n \approx 1{,}000\), random sampling variability narrows into a tight cone around the continental mean (grey ribbon). Regional estimates of \(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\) (chl_a, top row) stay tightly clustered inside the random-sampling cone, whereas ecoregion-specific slopes for \(\alpha_{\text{DOC}}\) (doc, middle row) and \(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\) (tss_dead, bottom row) spread well outside the random-sampling envelope even at \(n > 10{,}000\). That spread reflects genuine regional differences in dissolved organic matter aromaticity (Spencer et al. 2012; Griffin et al. 2018) and suspended particle size and mineralogy (Dodds & Whiles 2004; Gohin et al. 2005). Section 8 Continental Application & Dominance Regimes (apply_model7()) 8.1 Continental 3-Constituent Application Dataset Once Model 7 is calibrated on the 276,321 four-variable training matchups, it requires only the three constituent concentrations (\(\text{NAP}\), \(\text{DOC}\), and \(\text{Chl }a\)) to partition non-water light attenuation. Under our asymmetric “odd-one-out” rule (Rule 2), when Secchi depth is much shallower than the three constituents imply (\(z_r > +2.5\text{ SD}\), 3,496 matchups, mostly clear, shallow streams), only the secchi field is set to NA so the 3-constituent chemistry is retained with a modeled Secchi depth. Conversely, records where Secchi depth is much deeper than the constituents imply (\(z_r < -2.5\text{ SD}\), 1,622 records) are dropped. Applying Model 7 across all simultaneous 3-constituent matchups within the training concentration bounds yields 484,723 observations across 39,595 stations. No record is dropped for its NAP value. Where the algal dry mass estimated from Chl a equals or exceeds TSS (4,788 records, 1.0%), the non-algal mass is below what TSS can resolve, so NAP is drawn below the TSS reporting limit of 0.5 mg L⁻¹ in the same way as measured values below their limits (Section 4).
